days.context_before:
This is the final day of the journey. The last reading of the last book of the Bible.

You'll see the new Jerusalem in detail — its gates, its foundations, its strange and beautiful materials. You'll see the river of life flowing through its streets. You'll see the tree of life — the same tree from Genesis 3, the one humans were exiled from with a flaming sword — replanted in the middle of the city, with leaves for the healing of the nations.

This is no accident. The Bible begins with humans in a garden, near the tree of life, in the presence of God. The Bible ends with humans in a garden-city, eating from the tree of life, seeing God's face. The exile that began at Genesis 3 ends here. The story comes home.

Then Jesus speaks his last words in Scripture: "Yes, I am coming quickly." John responds with the prayer the church has prayed ever since: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus."

The Bible ends with one final sentence — short, quiet, complete: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen."

Read today's passage slowly. You have walked a very long way. You are about to arrive home.
days.plain_english_simple:
This is the last reading. The final scene of the Bible.

An angel takes John to a high mountain and shows him the city — the new Jerusalem — coming down from God. It is breathtaking. Gates of pearl. Walls of jasper. Streets of pure gold so refined it looks like clear glass. The city is enormous and luminous, glowing with the very presence of God.

Look at what the city does NOT have:

• No temple — because God himself is its temple
• No sun, no moon — because God's glory is the light
• No night — only endless day
• No curse — the curse from Genesis 3 is finally undone

A river flows from the throne, through the middle of the street. On both sides of the river stands the tree of life — the same tree from Genesis 3. Remember? When Adam and Eve were exiled from the garden, an angel with a flaming sword was placed at the entrance to keep them away from the tree of life. The exile lasted the entire Bible.

Here, at the end, the tree is back. "Its leaves are for the healing of the nations." Every wound that history has inflicted — finally healed.

And one more line worth lingering on: "They will see his face." Throughout the whole Bible, no one could see God's face and live. Here, finally, they do. Face to face with God.

Then Jesus speaks his last words in the Bible:

"Behold, I come quickly... Yes, I come quickly."

And John gives the answer the church has been giving ever since:

"Amen. Come, Lord Jesus."

The Bible's final sentence is short and warm. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen."

The journey is complete.
days.plain_english_standard:
Today is the final reading of the entire journey. The last words of the last book of the Bible.

**The city revealed.** An angel takes John up to a great and high mountain — the same posture in which Moses received the Law at Sinai, the same posture in which prophets received visions. From the mountain, John sees the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God.

The city is described in the language of unimaginable beauty. It shines with the very glory of God like the most precious of stones — jasper, clear as crystal. It has twelve gates, named for the twelve tribes of Israel. It has twelve foundations, named for the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The whole people of God across both covenants is built into the very structure of the eternal city.

The details accumulate. The walls are jasper. The city itself is pure gold, transparent like glass. The twelve gates are each one massive pearl. The streets are pure gold like clear glass. Don't try to picture this literally — it is meant to communicate that the eternal home of God's people is beautiful beyond imagining.

**What the city does NOT have.** The most striking features of the new Jerusalem are what is missing:

• "I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple." Every place of worship Israel ever built — the tabernacle in the wilderness, the temple of Solomon, the rebuilt temple after exile — was a placeholder for direct access to God. In the new creation, the placeholder is gone, because the reality has arrived. God himself is the temple.

• "The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb." The first thing God created in Genesis 1 was light. The last image of the city is a place where God's own light has replaced the sun.

• "There will be no night there." The fear and uncertainty of darkness, which has shaped human life since the first night, is gone.

• "There will be no curse any more." The curse of Genesis 3 — pain, futility, alienation, death — is fully reversed.

• The gates never close. In the ancient world, city gates were shut at night for protection. The new Jerusalem's gates stay open forever because there is nothing left to fear.

**The tree of life replanted.** Revelation 22:1-2 contains one of the most stunning images in the entire Bible. A river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, down the middle of the city's main street. On both sides of the river stands the tree of life.

This is the same tree from Genesis 3. When Adam and Eve sinned, they were exiled from the garden, and cherubim with a flaming sword were placed at the entrance to guard the way to the tree of life. Humanity has been on the outside of that tree for the entire rest of Scripture.

Here, at the end, the tree is back. Not behind a sword. Not in a garden walled off. Planted in the middle of the city, beside the river, accessible to everyone who belongs to the Lamb. Its leaves are "for the healing of the nations."

The whole arc of the Bible bends here. Genesis 3: exile, tree lost, sword guarding. Revelation 22: return, tree restored, sword put away, healing for every nation.

**"They will see his face."** Throughout the entire Bible, no one could see God's face and live. Moses asked, and God showed him only his back. The patriarchs encountered angels and theophanies but never the unveiled face of God. In the new creation, the limit is finally lifted: "They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads." Face to face with God, marked as his own, forever.

**Jesus' last words in Scripture.** As the Bible closes, Jesus speaks one last time. Three times in the closing verses, he says some form of: "I come quickly." These are the last recorded words of Jesus in the whole of Scripture.

John's response is the response the church has prayed for two thousand years: "Amen. Yes, come, Lord Jesus."

**The final sentence of the Bible.** And then, after sixty-six books and centuries of story, the Bible's last sentence:

"The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen."

Grace. Jesus. With his people. Amen.

That is the last word. That is how the story ends.

You have walked the whole journey. May you walk on with God.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Today's reading is the climactic conclusion of the entire biblical story. The literary, theological, and pastoral richness of Revelation 21-22 deserves careful attention.

**The vision from the mountain.** John is taken "in the Spirit" to a great and high mountain. This is the same posture in which Moses received the Law (Exodus 19) and Ezekiel received his temple vision (Ezekiel 40). High mountains in Scripture are places of meeting between God and his servants. The angel's invitation — "Come here. I will show you the wife, the Lamb's bride" — picks up the bridal imagery introduced in 21:2. The city is the bride; the eternal community of God's people is presented as the beloved of Christ.

**The architecture of the city.** The numerical structure is theologically dense. Twelve gates, each named for a tribe of Israel; twelve foundations, each named for an apostle of the Lamb. Twelve squared (144) appears in the dimensions and the wall thickness. The city is described as a cube — equal in length, breadth, and height (21:16). The only other cube in Scripture is the Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20). The implication is striking: the entire eternal city is the Holy of Holies. The place where only the high priest could enter once a year, on the Day of Atonement, after elaborate cleansing — that place is now the home of all God's people forever.

**The materials.** The accumulation of precious stones and gold is not meant to fund a literal architectural calculation. It is meant to communicate transcendent beauty — wealth beyond imagining, used not for hoarding but for the eternal home of all who belong to God. The jasper of the walls echoes the jasper of God's throne in chapter 4. The pearls — typically used for one bead at a time — are here each massive enough to form a city gate. The gold is so refined it is transparent. The point is the visual: you cannot picture how beautiful this is.

**"I saw no temple."** This is one of the most theologically loaded statements in the chapter. Every temple Israel ever built was provisional — a structure to mediate the presence of God to a people who could not bear his unmediated presence. In the new creation, the mediation is no longer needed. "The Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple." God's presence fills the city the way the glory once filled the tabernacle and the temple — but now without veil, without limit, without separation.

**The light.** "The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine." Genesis 1 begins with God creating light, then later setting the sun and moon to govern day and night. In the new creation, the intermediaries are no longer needed. God's own light illuminates everything. Day and night, sleep and waking, the rhythms that ordered the old creation are no longer required. There is only endless day. "Its lamp is the Lamb."

**The open gates and the nations.** "Its gates will in no way be shut by day (for there will be no night there)." The eternal city is welcoming, not closed. "The nations will walk in its light. The kings of the earth bring the glory and honor of the nations into it." Some Christians have read this as a hint of universal salvation; the more common faithful reading sees it as the picture of every people-group of the redeemed bringing their distinct cultural beauty into the eternal city. The new creation is not monocultural. The richness of every nation, healed of every brokenness, finds its place in the worship of the Lamb.

**The river and the tree.** Revelation 22:1-2 is the deliberate closing of the Bible's longest narrative arc. The river of the water of life flows from the throne. On both banks stands the tree of life. The same tree from Genesis 2-3 — the tree humans were exiled from, the tree Adam and Eve could no longer eat from after the fall — is here, replanted, accessible, fruit-bearing, healing.

This is the literary masterpiece of the Bible. Read together:
  - Genesis 1: God creates heaven and earth. Revelation 21: a new heaven and a new earth.
  - Genesis 1-2: a garden with the tree of life. Revelation 22: a garden-city with the tree of life replanted.
  - Genesis 3: humans exiled, cherubim guard with flaming sword. Revelation 21-22: humans welcomed, gates open, no curse.
  - Genesis 3: the serpent. Revelation 20: the serpent finally and fully defeated.
  - Genesis 3: shame, hiding, separation from God. Revelation 22: "They will see his face."
  - Genesis 11: nations scattered at Babel, languages confused. Revelation 7: every nation, tribe, people, and language unified in worship.

The Bible is one story. It ends where it began — only better, because what was lost is now restored, and what was simple is now mature.

**"The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations."** The healing language is significant. The Greek word *therapeia* is where we get our word "therapy." The leaves of the eternal tree are not for resurrecting people already in the new creation (they are already free from death). The healing is for the wounds of history. Every centuries-long enmity, every ancestral injustice, every cultural trauma — all of it healed. The nations that were scattered, then enslaved, then warred, then crucified each other across history all find their wounds tended at the tree.

**"There will be no curse any more."** This single sentence reverses the most consequential moment in the Bible's first chapters. The curse of Genesis 3 — pain, futility, thorns, sweat, alienation, death — is comprehensively undone. The Greek *katathema* (curse, banned thing) carries the sense of something devoted to destruction. In the new creation, nothing exists that is under such a ban. All things are blessed.

**"They will see his face."** Throughout Scripture, seeing God's face was simultaneously the deepest human longing and the most dangerous human prospect. Moses asked to see God's face; God showed him only his back, "for no man may see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Isaiah, glimpsing the throne, cried out that he was undone (Isaiah 6:5). The fulfilled longing of every faithful human heart — to behold God's face directly, fully, eternally — is realized here. The vision of God (what Christian tradition has called the *visio Dei* or the *beatific vision*) is the eternal home of God's people.

**Jesus' last words.** The Bible records Jesus speaking three times in the closing verses of Revelation: 22:12 ("Behold, I come quickly"), 22:13 ("I am the Alpha and the Omega"), 22:16 (identifying himself as the root and offspring of David, the bright morning star), and 22:20 ("Yes, I come quickly"). These are the last recorded words of Jesus in all of Scripture. The recurring promise of his coming is not a threat; it is a comfort. To those who love him and have waited long, the promise of his return is the dearest possible word.

**"Amen. Yes, come, Lord Jesus."** John's response — *amen, erchou, kyrie Iesou* — is one of the earliest recorded prayers of the Christian church. The Aramaic version (*Maranatha* — "Our Lord, come") was used in early Christian worship (1 Corinthians 16:22). The church across two thousand years has continued to pray this same prayer.

**The final benediction.** "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen." The Bible ends not with a thunderclap of judgment but with a quiet word of grace. The last word is *grace*. The last name is *Jesus*. The last description of those receiving the blessing is *all the saints* — everyone set apart by God across history and into eternity. The last syllable is *amen* — let it be so.

From Genesis to Revelation, this is how the story closes. Grace. Jesus. With his people. Forever.

You have walked the whole road. May you walk on with God.
days.key_insight: The exile that began at Genesis 3 ends here. The tree of life lost in Eden is replanted in the eternal city. The story of the Bible comes home — and Jesus' last words are: "Yes, I come quickly."
days.reflection_prompt: You have just finished walking the whole story — from the first "Let there be light" to the last "Yes, come, Lord Jesus." What part of the journey has stayed with you most? What do you want to carry forward into the rest of your life with God?
days.application_action: Today, take a quiet ten minutes. Thank God for the journey. Pray the prayer John prayed: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." Then ask God what one thing he wants you to keep walking in tomorrow.

confusion_topics.topic: How does Revelation connect back to Genesis?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: The Bible is a single story with deliberate bookends. Watch the parallels: Genesis begins with "a new heaven and a new earth" being created; Revelation ends with "a new heaven and a new earth" being renewed. Genesis has a garden with the tree of life; Revelation has a garden-city with the tree of life. Genesis has humans exiled from God's presence with a flaming sword guarding the way back; Revelation has humans welcomed, the gates open, the curse lifted. Genesis 11 scattered the nations at Babel; Revelation 7 gathers every nation, tribe, and language in unified worship. The Bible begins with humans walking with God in a garden and ends with humans seeing God face to face in a city. Everything in between is the story of how God brings his people home. That structure is not accidental — it is the Bible's deepest claim about reality.

confusion_topics.topic: Why is there a city instead of a garden?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Genesis 1-2 starts with a garden. Revelation 21-22 ends with a garden-city. This is not a downgrade; it is a maturing. A city implies community, culture, art, work, governance, gathering — the fullness of what humans, made in God's image, were always meant to create. The new Jerusalem is the garden filled in by all the goodness humanity has produced under God across history. The story moves from individuals in a garden (Adam and Eve) to a multitude in a city — every nation, every tribe, every language. The eternal home of God's people is not just paradise restored. It is paradise matured.

confusion_topics.topic: What does it mean that "the nations" walk in the city's light?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Revelation 21:24 says "the nations will walk in its light" and 22:2 says the leaves of the tree are "for the healing of the nations." The vision is striking: the new creation includes the redeemed of every people group, every culture, every language. The kings of the earth bring the glory and honor of the nations into the city — meaning, in the most likely reading, that the unique beauty of every culture (its languages, its arts, its distinctives) is brought into the eternal community of God. The new creation is gloriously multicultural. The nations are not erased; they are healed and gathered.

confusion_topics.topic: Why does the Bible end with Jesus saying "I come quickly" if he hasn't come back in 2,000 years?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: The Greek word *tachu* (translated "quickly") can mean "soon" or "suddenly." It does not necessarily mean "within a few years." The New Testament consistently treats the time between Christ's resurrection and his return as "the last days" (Acts 2:17, Hebrews 1:2, 1 John 2:18) — meaning the final era of history, however long it lasts. 2 Peter 3:8-9 addresses this question directly: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promise... but is patient with us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." The delay is mercy — time for more people to come home. The promise still stands.

confusion_topics.topic: What does it mean to "see God's face"?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Throughout the Bible, seeing God's face directly was simultaneously the deepest human longing and impossibly dangerous. Moses asked, and God showed him only his back, saying "no man may see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). The reason is not that God is hiding — it is that fallen, mortal humans cannot bear the unmediated presence of holy God. In the new creation, when believers have been resurrected and the curse is lifted, the limit is finally removed. "They will see his face." This is the fulfillment of every spiritual longing — direct, unmediated, eternal communion with God himself. Christian tradition has called this 'the beatific vision' — the seeing that completes the human heart.

days.retention_anchor: You have walked the entire story. From Genesis 1's "In the beginning, God created" to Revelation 22's "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen." The garden became the city. The tree lost in Eden was replanted by the river. The exile ended. The story came home. You finished the journey. May you walk on with God — knowing now how it all begins, and how it all ends, and the One who holds it all together.
